title: Cicero on duties
hook: Cicero, not a Stoic himself, wrote On Duties drawing on Panaetius (On Duties 1)

segments.voice: Yesterday: sympatheia, the bond Posidonius saw linking the ocean to the moon. Your line was the moon and tides. Did you find the moon last night? Day six hundred forty-six.

A father writes to his son, who's away at university in another country. The son, the letters hint, has been spending more time at parties than in lectures. The father's city has just been through an assassination, and danger is closing in around him. He doesn't write a scolding letter. He writes a book, in three parts, on how to live as a decent person in public life. It will outlast him by a long way. Today: officium.
screen: `A FATHER WRITES TO HIS SON.` → `ROME, AFTER AN ASSASSINATION.` → `A BOOK ON HOW TO LIVE.`

segments.voice: First, the writer. Marcus Tullius Cicero was a Roman orator and statesman. He was not a Stoic. In philosophy he belonged to the Academy, the school descended from Plato, which taught that we should hold our views with caution. But he admired the Stoics' ethics, and he borrowed freely. Second, the moment. In the year 44 BC, after Julius Caesar was assassinated, Cicero wrote On Duties for his son, also named Marcus, who was studying in Athens. The book has three parts. What is honorable. What is useful. And what to do when the two seem to clash. Third, the borrowing. For the first two parts, Cicero says plainly that he's following Panaetius, the Stoic we met two days ago, but as his own judge, not just as a translator. Panaetius had promised a third part on the clash between honor and usefulness, and never wrote it. Cicero did. His answer is firm: a thing that's truly dishonorable can never really be useful. If it looks useful, you're looking wrong. Fourth, the cost. A year later, Cicero was killed on the orders of Mark Antony, whom he had attacked in speeches. He didn't get to see what his son became. But the book lasted. Readers kept copying and studying it long after Rome fell. The Latin word in the title, officium, means duty, but also service, a job done for others. A duty, to Cicero, wasn't a weight. It was what a person owes as a citizen, a friend, a parent.
screen: `CICERO: NOT A STOIC, A BORROWER.` · `44 BC: A BOOK FOR HIS SON.` · `PANAETIUS, PLUS A THIRD PART.` · `OFFICIUM: DUTY AS SERVICE.` · then, large: `ON DUTIES.`

segments.voice: Sit, and breathe. Think of the roles you hold right now: maybe child, parent, partner, coworker, neighbor, friend. Pick one. Ask Cicero's question: what does this role ask of me today? Not everything. One duty. Picking up the phone. Finishing the report honestly. Listening without the screen. Let it be specific. Now picture yourself doing it well, the way you'd want it done for you. The bell holds the time.
Officium. Cicero's Latin word for duty: a service owed to others, as a citizen, a friend, a parent. Today's word.
Your line: on duties. Do your one chosen duty today, well and fully, as a service, not a chore. Day six hundred forty-six.

howItsDone: Students of ethics and political thought read Cicero's On Duties as a guide to public and private obligation, and as a main window onto the Stoic idea of fitting action.

original.note: Latin: duty, service, a job owed to others. Cicero's word for the Greek kathēkon.

trapdoor: what you thought: On Duties is a Stoic book.
what it means: a book by Cicero, an Academic, for his son, built on the Stoic Panaetius with a third part of his own.
what a scholar hears: De Officiis (44 BC) is a main source for Panaetius's lost Peri tou kathēkontos, and it shaped medieval and Renaissance moral education.
recall: an army base on the Danube

notes: Cicero born January 106 BC, so 62 in autumn 44 BC when he wrote On Duties. Confirm.
Young Marcus's partying in Athens: attested in letters (e.g. Cicero, Ad Familiares 16.21 from the son, and reports to Atticus). Hedged 'by most accounts'; confirm.
Cicero says he follows Panaetius not as a translator but correcting where he judges (On Duties 1.6, 2.60, 3.7). Confirm.
Panaetius's promised third part never written: On Duties 3.7–10. Confirm.
Cicero killed 7 December 43 BC on Antony's proscription. Confirm.
